newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ celebrates 10th anniversary of nuclear-free law.
newsitem.headline: NZ celebrates 10th anniversary of nuclear-free law.

text.p: New Zealand marked the tenth anniversary of its controversial nuclear-free policy on Sunday with a pledge to help rid the world of all nuclear weapons.

A decade after the small South Pacific nation passed the world's first statute preventing nuclear-armed and powered ships from visiting its shores, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said New Zealand would remain at the forefront of the drive to eliminate nuclear weapons.

"There is still a long way to go. New Zealand, for one, wants to see negotiations start this year on a cut-off treaty to halt the production of the fissile materials used to make nuclear weapons," Bolger said in a speech to the Institute of International Affairs.

"We want to see the nuclear weapons states live up to their obligations, under the nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, to pursue and bring to a conclusion negotiations leading to complete nuclear disarmament.
"In today's world, there can be no logical justification for the use of nuclear weapons," he said.

A handful of opposition Labour Party politicians and anti-nuclear supporters gathered on the steps of Parliament to commemorate the passage of the New Zealand Nuclear Free Zone, Disarmament and Arms Control Act, passed by the fourth Labour government in 1987.
A yellow "peace rose" was planted in Parliament grounds.
"We are a small country at the bottom of the world that took a stand...a stand on nuclear arms, the arms race and for peace," Labour parliamentarian Annette King said.
"That legislation was the final part of the stand."
Labour, under the leadership of David Lange, banned all nuclear-armed and powered vessels from New Zealand ports when it came to power in 1984.
The policy soured relations with many countries, particularly Washington, which in 1986 suspended New Zealand from the ANZUS tripartite defence alliance with Australia.
The rift between the two allies deepened when the policy became law a year later and relations have only recently started to warm.
"Today it is popular to be anti-nuclear -- it wasn't always the case," King said.
"At the time, the British were furious, the United States were mad with us and the Australians, they were fuming.
"It was a turning point for New Zealand. We said there was nothing to be gained by having nuclear weapons providing security for this country."

But on the eve of the commemorations, Labour leader Helen Clark warned against complacency in maintaining the legislation and lashed out at the government, which she said would like to see nuclear-powered ships back in New Zealand ports.

"(Defence Minister) Paul East visited nuclear-powered warships in Hawaii a few months ago and has stated publicly that he would like to see them return to New Zealand," Clark told a Peace Studies Foundation seminar in Auckland.
"Labour believes that the admission of nuclear-powered warships to New Zealand would pose unnecessary risks to New Zealand.
"Our present legislation requires the prime minister to be satisfied that visiting warships are not nuclear-armed. All these features of our existing law must be upheld."
